lessons.title: Rhythms the first pass leaves out
lessons.body:
## The junction can steal, not just rescue

An escape rhythm appears because nothing faster is available. An **accelerated** rhythm appears because a lower focus started firing faster than the sinus node and took the beat away from it.

**Accelerated junctional rhythm** is regular and narrow at `60-100`, with P waves inverted in lead `II`, buried inside the QRS, or landing just after it. It is not a safety net, it is a sign: digoxin toxicity, inferior infarction, myocarditis, the first day after cardiac surgery, or theophylline.

**Isorhythmic AV dissociation** is what you see when the sinus node and the junction run at nearly the same rate. P waves drift slowly toward the QRS, vanish inside it, then reappear on the far side.

> **Key:** AV dissociation is not a synonym for complete heart block. In block the atrial rate is **faster** than the ventricular rate and P waves fail even when they land on ready tissue. In usurpation the ventricular rate is equal to or faster than the atrial rate, so no P ever gets a fair chance to conduct.

## Ectopic atrial tachycardia

One non-sinus atrial focus fires at `130-250`. The strip shows a **visible P wave of the wrong shape** in front of every QRS, a PR that may be normal or long, and an onset that **warms up** over several beats instead of starting between one beat and the next.

Adenosine usually just exposes the P waves by blocking the AV node without stopping the tachycardia, which is the opposite of what happens in AVNRT. Atrial tachycardia **with** AV block is the digoxin signature.

## Flutter that does not sit at 150

Flutter waves march at a fixed `250-350` per minute, usually near `300`. When the AV node alternates between `2:1`, `3:1` and `4:1` conduction, the ventricular response becomes irregular and gets mistaken for atrial fibrillation.

The tell is arithmetic. The F-to-F interval never changes, about `0.20` seconds, and every R-to-R interval is a whole multiple of it. Ventricular rates therefore cluster at `150`, `100` and `75` rather than scattering.

## A sinus node wearing out

**Sinus node dysfunction**, also called sick sinus syndrome, is a collection rather than one finding: inappropriate sinus bradycardia, sinus pauses, chronotropic incompetence where the rate will not rise with exertion, and **tachy-brady syndrome**, in which atrial fibrillation stops and is followed by a long pause before the sinus node wakes up.

Two pauses look alike and are not the same. In **sinoatrial exit block** the pause is an exact multiple of the underlying P-to-P interval, because a beat formed and never got out. In **sinus arrest** the pause bears no arithmetic relationship to it, because no beat formed at all. Either way, symptoms plus documented bradycardia is a permanent pacemaker conversation.

## Wide beats that are not ventricular

The right bundle has the longest refractory period, so a beat arriving too early can find it still recovering and conduct with a right bundle pattern. That is **rate-dependent**, or phase 3, aberrancy.

The named version is the **Ashman phenomenon**: in atrial fibrillation, a long R-to-R followed by a short one produces a single wide beat with an `RSR'` in `V1`. It looks like a PVC and is not one. The giveaway is the long-short sequence plus the right bundle shape.

## Two patterns to recognize on sight

**Bidirectional ventricular tachycardia:** the QRS axis flips beat to beat, alternating upright and inverted in the limb leads. The short list is digoxin toxicity, catecholaminergic polymorphic VT, and aconite poisoning.

**Pre-excited atrial fibrillation:** irregularly irregular, wide, and very fast, with the **QRS width changing from beat to beat** as the share of each beat conducted down the accessory pathway varies. A shortest R-to-R under `250 ms`, or rates above `250`, makes it nearly diagnostic.

> **Trap:** Pre-excited atrial fibrillation is the one irregular wide tachycardia where the usual rate-control drugs kill. Procainamide or electricity; never adenosine, beta blockers, calcium channel blockers or digoxin.
keyPoints: An accelerated junctional rhythm at 60-100 is usurpation, not escape, and points at digoxin, inferior MI, myocarditis, or recent cardiac surgery
AV dissociation by usurpation has a ventricular rate equal to or faster than the atrial rate; in complete block the atrial rate is faster
Atrial flutter with variable block is irregular, but the F-to-F interval stays fixed near 0.20 s and R-to-R intervals are whole multiples of it
Sinoatrial exit block gives a pause that is an exact multiple of the P-to-P interval; sinus arrest gives a pause with no arithmetic relationship
Pre-excited atrial fibrillation is irregular, wide, with beat-to-beat changing QRS width and R-R under 250 ms: procainamide or electricity only

checks.q: A strip in atrial fibrillation shows one wide beat with an RSR' in V1, and it follows a long R-to-R interval immediately succeeded by a short one. What is it?
choices: The Ashman phenomenon, aberrant conduction rather than a PVC
A unifocal PVC
A fusion beat proving ventricular tachycardia
Failure to capture from an implanted device
checks.why: A long-short cycle sequence plus a right bundle branch block shape is classic Ashman aberrancy. The right bundle has the longest refractory period, so an early beat after a long pause conducts down the left bundle only.

checks.q: How does an ectopic atrial tachycardia behave differently from AVNRT when adenosine is given?
choices: It converts immediately to sinus rhythm
It usually continues while the AV block reveals the abnormal P waves
It degenerates into ventricular fibrillation
It has no response at all because the AV node is not involved
checks.why: An automatic atrial focus keeps firing when the AV node is blocked, so adenosine exposes the P waves without terminating the rhythm. AVNRT uses the AV node as part of its circuit, so blocking it stops the tachycardia.

checks.q: P waves march at 96 and QRS complexes at 104, with the P waves slowly drifting into and out of the QRS. What is this?
choices: Complete heart block with a junctional escape
Mobitz II second-degree block
Isorhythmic AV dissociation from an accelerated junctional rhythm
Atrial flutter with variable conduction
checks.why: The ventricular rate exceeds the atrial rate, so no P wave ever arrives at ready tissue. Nothing is blocked; the junction simply outran the sinus node. In complete block the atria would be the faster of the two.

lessons.title: Localization, second pass: finding the culprit artery
lessons.body:
## The mirror shows up first

ST depression in `aVL` is frequently the **earliest** finding of an inferior occlusion, appearing while the inferior elevation is still unconvincing. `aVL` and lead `III` sit almost exactly opposite one another, roughly `150` degrees apart, which makes them the tightest reciprocal pair on the tracing.

In a patient with chest pain, any horizontal or downsloping depression in `aVL` earns a hard second look at `II`, `III` and `aVF` and a repeat tracing in `10` minutes.

## Right coronary or circumflex

Inferior elevation has two possible culprits, and separating them changes what happens next.

| Finding | Right coronary | Circumflex |
|---|---|---|
| Elevation, III versus II | `III` greater than `II` | `II` at least equal to `III` |
| ST in I and aVL | Depressed | Isoelectric or elevated |
| Lateral leads | Usually spared | Elevation in `V5-V6` common |
| Company it keeps | Bradycardia, AV block, right ventricular infarct | Posterior involvement |

## The right ventricle

Suspect right ventricular involvement in every inferior STEMI where `III` beats `II`. ST elevation in `V1` alongside inferior elevation is the clue available on a standard tracing. Confirm with **right-sided leads**: `0.5 mm` of elevation in `V4R` is diagnostic, `1 mm` in men under `30`.

The clinical triad is hypotension, clear lungs, and distended neck veins. These patients live on preload: give `500-1000 mL` of crystalloid, withhold nitrates and preload-reducing doses of morphine, and expect the heart block that travels with a proximal right coronary lesion.

## How proximal is the LAD

- **Proximal to the first septal perforator:** elevation in `V1-V4` **plus** `aVL`, reciprocal depression in `II, III, aVF`, often a new right bundle branch block with left anterior fascicular block, and ST elevation in `aVR`. The largest territory and the one that produces cardiogenic shock.
- **Distal LAD:** anterior elevation without `aVL` involvement and without inferior reciprocal depression.
- **Wrap-around LAD:** anterior **and** inferior elevation together, which reads as contradictory until you know the vessel curls around the apex onto the inferior wall.

## High lateral, and the flag

Isolated elevation in `I` and `aVL` with reciprocal depression in `III` and `aVF` is a first diagonal or ramus occlusion. When elevation sits in `I`, `aVL` and `V2` while `III` is depressed, the leads form the pattern nicknamed the **South African flag sign**, and it means the first diagonal branch.

## Posterior, said precisely

Posterior, properly inferobasal, infarction shows up in `V1-V3` as four findings together: **horizontal ST depression**, an **R wave taller than the S wave is deep** in `V2`, an R wave `0.04` seconds or wider, and an **upright T wave**.

Depression that is maximal in `V2-V3` rather than spread evenly across the precordium is what separates it from ordinary subendocardial ischemia. Confirm with `V7-V9`, where `0.5 mm` of elevation is diagnostic.

## Four cases, read by the mirror

1. `2 mm` elevation in `II, III, aVF` with `III` larger than `II`, `2 mm` depression in `I` and `aVL`, `1 mm` elevation in `V1`. **Proximal right coronary with right ventricular involvement.** Fluids, no nitrates, get `V4R`.
2. `3 mm` elevation `V2-V4`, `1.5 mm` elevation in `aVL`, `1 mm` depression in `II, III, aVF`. **Proximal LAD.**
3. `2 mm` horizontal depression `V1-V3` with a tall R in `V2` and upright T waves, plus `1 mm` elevation in `II, III, aVF`. **Inferoposterior.** Get `V7-V9`.
4. `1.5 mm` elevation in `I` and `aVL` only, `1 mm` depression in `III`. **First diagonal.** A small territory is still an occlusion.

> **Trap:** Territory size is not the same as urgency. A first diagonal occlusion involves few leads and still closes an artery, and a posterior infarct shows only depression on a standard tracing. Both get treated as occlusions.
keyPoints: ST depression in aVL is often the earliest sign of inferior occlusion, because aVL and III are the tightest reciprocal pair on the ECG
Inferior elevation with III greater than II and depression in I and aVL means right coronary; II at least equal to III with lateral changes means circumflex
Right ventricular infarct: elevation in V1 with inferior elevation, confirmed by 0.5 mm in V4R, treated with fluid and no nitrates
Proximal LAD gives anterior elevation plus aVL elevation, inferior reciprocal depression, and sometimes new RBBB with left anterior fascicular block
Posterior infarct is horizontal depression in V1-V3 with a tall R in V2, an R wave 0.04 s or wider, and upright T waves; confirm with V7-V9

checks.q: A tracing shows 2 mm ST elevation in II, III and aVF, with III clearly larger than II, and 2 mm depression in I and aVL. Which vessel and which extra lead set?
choices: Left circumflex; get posterior leads V7-V9
Right coronary; get right-sided leads including V4R
Left anterior descending; get a repeat standard 12-lead
First diagonal; no additional leads needed
checks.why: III greater than II with reciprocal depression in I and aVL points at the right coronary artery, which raises the chance of right ventricular involvement. V4R with 0.5 mm of elevation confirms it and changes fluid and nitrate decisions.

checks.q: Which set of findings in V1 to V3 indicates a posterior infarction rather than anterior subendocardial ischemia?
choices: Upsloping depression with flattened T waves spread evenly across all six precordial leads
Convex ST elevation with deep Q waves
Horizontal depression maximal in V2-V3 with a tall R wave and upright T waves
Deeply inverted symmetric T waves with preserved R waves
checks.why: A posterior infarct is a mirror image: depression instead of elevation, a tall R instead of a deep Q, and an upright T instead of an inverted one, concentrated in V2-V3. Deep symmetric T inversions in V2-V3 would instead suggest Wellens.

lessons.title: The pediatric ECG and what counts as normal by age
lessons.body:
## A newborn's heart is right-dominant

Before birth the right ventricle pumps against the resistance of the whole body, so a newborn's ECG is a right ventricular ECG. By adult standards it looks abnormal, and it is not.

- **Axis** at birth runs `+60` to `+180` degrees. It migrates leftward over the first months and reaches the adult `0` to `+90` range by roughly age `3`.
- **Tall R waves in `V1`** are normal in the newborn, with an R-to-S ratio greater than `1` that falls as the child grows.
- **The T wave in `V1`** is upright for the first week, **inverts by about day `7`**, and stays inverted until somewhere between age `7` and adolescence. That is the **juvenile T wave pattern**.

> **Key:** An upright T wave in `V1` between one week and roughly seven years of age is abnormal and suggests right ventricular hypertrophy. It is the single most useful pediatric normal to memorize.

## Numbers that shrink as the child grows

| Age | Resting rate | PR upper limit | QRS upper limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Newborn | `110-160` | `0.12 s` | `0.07 s` |
| 1-2 years | `100-150` | `0.13 s` | `0.07 s` |
| 3-5 years | `80-120` | `0.15 s` | `0.08 s` |
| 6-12 years | `70-110` | `0.16 s` | `0.09 s` |
| Adolescent | `60-100` | `0.18 s` | `0.10 s` |

Corrected QT thresholds do **not** shrink with age. Over `450 ms` deserves attention, over `460-470 ms` is prolonged, and over `500 ms` carries torsades risk exactly as in an adult.

Marked **sinus arrhythmia** is normal and often dramatic in school-age children. An `RSR'` in `V1` with a **narrow** QRS is a normal variant; the same pattern with a wide QRS or right axis deviation suggests an atrial septal defect.

## Sinus tachycardia or SVT in an infant

Sinus tachycardia in an infant rarely exceeds `220`, and in a child over one year rarely exceeds `180`. It also varies beat to beat and moves with fever, pain, and fluid.

Supraventricular tachycardia in an infant is **`220-300`**, monotonously regular with no beat-to-beat variation, P waves absent or abnormal, and the history is poor feeding, pallor and irritability rather than an obvious trigger.

The doses:

- **Adenosine `0.1 mg/kg`** rapid push, maximum `6 mg`, then `0.2 mg/kg`, maximum `12 mg`.
- **Synchronized cardioversion `0.5-1 J/kg`**, then `2 J/kg`.
- **Defibrillation `2 J/kg`**, then `4 J/kg`, subsequent shocks `4-10 J/kg` without exceeding the adult dose.

## Bradycardia in a child is a breathing problem

Children cannot raise stroke volume much, so cardiac output is rate-dependent and a slow child is a dying child. A heart rate under `60` with poor perfusion in an infant or child is treated with **oxygen, effective ventilation, and chest compressions**, because the cause is nearly always hypoxia.

Epinephrine `0.01 mg/kg IV or IO` of the `0.1 mg/mL` concentration follows. Atropine `0.02 mg/kg`, minimum dose `0.1 mg`, is reserved for vagally mediated bradycardia and AV block, not for hypoxia.

## Patterns worth knowing in children

- **Wolff-Parkinson-White:** short PR with a delta wave, associated with Ebstein anomaly, and a common substrate for infant SVT.
- **Long QT syndrome:** syncope with exertion, swimming, or a startling noise; a family history of sudden death or unexplained drowning; congenital deafness in the Jervell and Lange-Nielsen form.
- **Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy:** large voltages with deep narrow lateral Q waves in an adolescent with exertional syncope.
- **Myocarditis:** low voltage, diffuse ST and T changes, and ectopy in a child who was recently unwell.

> **Trap:** A computer interpretation on a pediatric tracing is frequently read against adult norms. Right axis, a tall R in `V1`, and an inverted T in `V1` are normal childhood findings that the machine may flag.
keyPoints: A newborn ECG is right-dominant: axis up to +180 degrees and tall R waves in V1, normalizing over the first few years
The T wave in V1 inverts by day 7 and stays inverted until about age 7; an upright T in V1 in that window suggests right ventricular hypertrophy
PR and QRS upper limits are shorter in children, but QTc thresholds are the same as adults, with over 500 ms high risk
Infant SVT is 220-300 and metronome-regular; infant sinus tachycardia rarely exceeds 220 and varies with fever, pain and volume
Bradycardia under 60 with poor perfusion in a child gets oxygen, ventilation and compressions first, because the cause is hypoxia

checks.q: A 3-year-old has an inverted T wave in V1 on an ECG done for a murmur. What does this mean?
choices: Normal for age, part of the juvenile T wave pattern
Anterior ischemia requiring troponins
Right ventricular hypertrophy
Lead misplacement
checks.why: The T wave in V1 inverts around day 7 and stays inverted until roughly age 7 or later. The abnormal finding in that age window is an upright T wave in V1, which suggests right ventricular hypertrophy.

checks.q: A 4-month-old is pale and feeding poorly with a regular narrow tachycardia at 270 that does not vary beat to beat. What is the first drug and dose?
choices: Amiodarone 5 mg/kg over 20 minutes
Adenosine 0.1 mg/kg rapid IV push, maximum 6 mg
Atropine 0.02 mg/kg IV
Digoxin 10 mcg/kg IV loading dose
checks.why: A rate of 270 with no beat-to-beat variation in an infant is SVT, not sinus tachycardia, which rarely exceeds 220 in infants. Adenosine 0.1 mg/kg then 0.2 mg/kg is first line in a perfusing infant; cardioversion at 0.5-1 J/kg is next.

checks.q: A 2-year-old with bronchiolitis has a heart rate of 48 with mottled skin and weak pulses. What is done first?
choices: Atropine 0.02 mg/kg IV
Transcutaneous pacing
Oxygen and effective ventilation, then compressions if the rate stays under 60 with poor perfusion
Epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg IV before any airway maneuver
checks.why: Pediatric bradycardia is nearly always hypoxic in origin, so oxygenation and ventilation come first and compressions start at a rate under 60 with poor perfusion. Epinephrine follows; atropine is for vagal causes and AV block.

lessons.title: Pacemakers and ICDs: the code, the modes, the failures
lessons.body:
## The NBG code

Devices are described by a five-letter code, and most conversations use only the first three.

| Position | Meaning | Letters |
|---|---|---|
| I | Chamber **paced** | `A`, `V`, `D`, `O` |
| II | Chamber **sensed** | `A`, `V`, `D`, `O` |
| III | **Response** to a sensed event | `I` inhibit, `T` trigger, `D` both, `O` none |
| IV | **Rate** modulation | `R` |
| V | Multisite pacing | `A`, `V`, `D` |

- `VVI`: paces the ventricle, senses the ventricle, and an intrinsic beat inhibits the next paced one. The workhorse for atrial fibrillation with a slow response.
- `AAI`: atrium only, appropriate when the sinus node is sick but AV conduction is intact.
- `DDD`: paces and senses both chambers, so it can track the patient's own atrium.
- `DOO` and `VOO`: asynchronous, no sensing at all. This is what a magnet produces and what you want during electrocautery.
- `VDD`: senses both chambers, paces only the ventricle, following the patient's own P waves.

## Reading a dual-chamber strip

Four combinations appear, often on the same tracing.

1. Atrial spike then a P, ventricular spike then a wide QRS. Both chambers paced.
2. Atrial spike then a P, then the patient's own narrow QRS. AV conduction is intact and the ventricular output was inhibited.
3. The patient's own P, then a ventricular spike and a wide QRS. Atrial tracking, also called P-synchronous pacing.
4. The patient's own P and own QRS with no spikes at all. Fully inhibited.

A right ventricular paced QRS looks like a **left bundle branch block with left axis**, because the lead sits at the right ventricular apex. A paced QRS with a **tall R wave in `V1`** means the left ventricle is being paced, which is what a biventricular resynchronization device should look like. Losing that R wave means the left ventricular lead stopped capturing.

## The failures

- **Failure to capture:** a spike with no P or QRS after it. Lead dislodgement or fracture, a rising threshold at the lead tip, **hyperkalemia**, class I antiarrhythmics, infarction under the lead, or battery depletion. Raising output or fixing the potassium restores it.
- **Failure to sense, or undersensing:** spikes appear where the device should have been inhibited, marching into and sometimes landing on the patient's own beats. The danger is a spike on a T wave. Causes are lead displacement, a low-amplitude intrinsic signal, an insulation break, or sensitivity set too low.
- **Oversensing:** the device counts something that is not a beat and withholds pacing, producing pauses. T-wave oversensing, muscle potentials from the diaphragm or chest wall, electromagnetic interference, and a fractured lead making noise.
- **Failure to output:** no spike where one belonged, usually from battery depletion, a fractured lead, or oversensing.

## Pacemaker-mediated tachycardia

A dual-chamber device with intact retrograde conduction can chase its own echo. A ventricular paced beat conducts backward into the atrium, the atrial channel senses that retrograde P, and the device paces the ventricle again. The result is a regular paced tachycardia sitting exactly at the device's **upper rate limit**, commonly `110-130`. A magnet breaks it instantly.

## What a magnet does

| Device | With a magnet applied |
|---|---|
| Pacemaker | Asynchronous pacing, `DOO` or `VOO`, at the **magnet rate**, often `85-100`; a reduced magnet rate near `65` signals battery replacement time |
| ICD | **Suspends shock therapy only**, with pacing function unchanged |

> **Trap:** A magnet on a pacemaker removes all sensing, so it will pace into the patient's own T waves. It is a short-term fix for a device that is pausing or chasing itself, not something to leave in place.

## ICD shocks

An appropriate shock treats a real ventricular arrhythmia. An **inappropriate shock** comes from atrial fibrillation with a fast response, sinus tachycardia above the programmed rate cutoff, T-wave oversensing, or noise from a fractured lead.

**Electrical storm** is three or more shocks in `24` hours. It is an emergency: interrogate the device, beta-blockade, usually amiodarone, sedation, and treat the trigger, which is often ischemia, heart failure or low potassium.
keyPoints: NBG positions: chamber paced, chamber sensed, response to sensing, rate modulation, multisite; VVI, AAI, DDD and VOO cover most conversations
A right ventricular paced beat looks like left bundle branch block with left axis; a tall R in V1 on a paced beat means the left ventricle is being paced
Failure to capture is a spike with no complex, and hyperkalemia is a reversible cause worth checking before blaming the lead
Undersensing puts spikes where they do not belong and risks a spike on a T wave; oversensing withholds pacing and produces pauses
A magnet makes a pacemaker asynchronous at its magnet rate and only suspends shock therapy on an ICD; three shocks in 24 hours is electrical storm

checks.q: In the NBG code, what does the third letter describe?
choices: Which chamber is sensed
Whether rate modulation is enabled
How the device responds to a sensed event
Which chamber is paced
checks.why: Position I is the chamber paced, position II the chamber sensed, and position III the response to sensing: I for inhibited, T for triggered, D for both, O for none. Rate modulation is position IV.

checks.q: A patient with a dual-chamber pacemaker has a regular paced tachycardia at exactly 125 that stops the moment a magnet is placed. What was it?
choices: Pacemaker-mediated tachycardia at the device's upper rate limit
Ventricular tachycardia
Failure to capture
Atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction
checks.why: A retrograde P sensed by the atrial channel triggers another paced ventricular beat, and the loop runs at the programmed upper rate limit. A magnet removes sensing, which breaks the loop instantly. Flutter and VT would not stop with a magnet.

checks.q: A dialysis patient with a pacemaker has spikes at 70 with several producing no QRS at all. Which reversible cause should be checked immediately?
choices: Oversensing of chest wall muscle potentials
Hyperkalemia raising the capture threshold
A magnet left on the device
Atrial tracking of a fast atrial rhythm
checks.why: Hyperkalemia raises the myocardial capture threshold and is a classic reversible cause of failure to capture, especially in a dialysis patient. Oversensing produces missing spikes rather than spikes without capture.

lessons.title: Eight rhythms, eight actions
lessons.body:
## Two questions choose the branch

The rhythm narrows the options. **Is there a pulse** and **is the patient stable** choose between them. Instability means hypotension, altered mental status, signs of shock, ischemic chest discomfort, or acute heart failure **caused by the rhythm**.

What follows is eight tracings and the action each one demands.

### 1. Coarse chaotic waveform, no QRS, no pulse

Ventricular fibrillation. **Defibrillate immediately** at `120-200 J` biphasic, resume compressions at once without a pulse check, epinephrine `1 mg` every `3-5` minutes, and amiodarone `300 mg` after the third shock followed by `150 mg`.

### 2. Wide regular complexes at 190, no pulse

Pulseless ventricular tachycardia is managed identically to fibrillation. It is shockable. The common error is spending time on a rhythm strip debate while compressions pause.

### 3. A flat line confirmed in two leads

Asystole. Check the gain and the electrode connections first, then high-quality CPR with **epinephrine `1 mg` as early as possible**, repeated every `3-5` minutes. Do not shock it. The work is hunting the reversible cause.

### 4. Organized narrow complexes at 130, no pulse

Pulseless electrical activity, and the shape of the complexes points at the cause. **Narrow and fast** suggests a filling or mechanical problem: hypovolemia, tamponade, tension pneumothorax, or pulmonary embolism. **Wide and slow** suggests a metabolic or toxic cause: hyperkalemia, sodium channel blockade, hypoxia, or severe acidosis. In a dialysis patient with wide slow PEA, give calcium empirically.

### 5. Regular narrow at 190, blood pressure 72/40, confused

Unstable supraventricular tachycardia. **Synchronized cardioversion** at `50-100 J`, with sedation if there is time. Adenosine is reasonable only if the line and the drug are already at the bedside and will not delay the shock.

### 6. Irregularly irregular at 165, blood pressure 80/48

Atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response causing shock. **Synchronized cardioversion** at `120-200 J`. Onset duration and anticoagulation status matter for elective cardioversion; instability overrides both.

### 7. Monomorphic wide at 165, blood pressure 128/76, talking

Stable ventricular tachycardia. Pads on, cardioversion ready, then an antiarrhythmic: **amiodarone `150 mg` over `10` minutes**, or **procainamide `20-50 mg/min`** until the arrhythmia stops, hypotension develops, the QRS widens by `50%`, or `17 mg/kg` is reached, or sotalol.

### 8. Polymorphic twisting complexes with a pulse and a QTc of 560

Torsades de pointes. **Magnesium sulfate `2 g IV`** over about `15` minutes, stop every QT-prolonging drug, replace potassium toward `4.5 mEq/L`, and use overdrive pacing or isoproterenol if it keeps recurring. If the pulse is lost, **unsynchronized defibrillation**, because the machine cannot synchronize to a shifting R wave.

> **Key:** Wide plus irregular is never synchronized. Polymorphic VT and pre-excited atrial fibrillation both get defibrillation doses, not sync.

## The bradycardia branch in one paragraph

Symptomatic bradycardia gets atropine `1 mg` every `3-5` minutes to a maximum of `3 mg`, then transcutaneous pacing, dopamine `5-20 mcg/kg/min`, or epinephrine `2-10 mcg/min`. In Mobitz II and in complete block with a wide escape, the lesion is below the AV node, so atropine usually fails and pacing should not wait for it.

> **On shift:** The rhythm on the monitor is a hypothesis until someone has a hand on a pulse. Every one of these eight actions starts with that touch.
keyPoints: Pulse and stability choose the algorithm branch; the rhythm only narrows the options within it
Shockable arrest is VF and pulseless VT: 120-200 J biphasic, epinephrine 1 mg every 3-5 minutes, amiodarone 300 mg then 150 mg
In PEA the complex shape points at the cause: narrow and fast means a filling problem, wide and slow means metabolic or toxic
Unstable tachycardia gets synchronized cardioversion at 50-100 J narrow, 120-200 J for atrial fibrillation, and 100 J for monomorphic VT
Torsades with a pulse gets magnesium 2 g IV and electrolyte correction; pulseless polymorphic VT gets unsynchronized defibrillation

checks.q: A dialysis patient arrests with organized wide complexes at 38 and no pulse. Beyond CPR and epinephrine, which empiric treatment is most appropriate?
choices: Immediate defibrillation at 200 J
Calcium for presumed hyperkalemia
Adenosine 6 mg rapid push
Synchronized cardioversion at 100 J
checks.why: Wide and slow PEA points at a metabolic or toxic cause, and in a dialysis patient hyperkalemia leads that list. Calcium stabilizes the membrane within minutes. PEA is not a shockable rhythm, so defibrillation and cardioversion do nothing.

checks.q: A patient with a pulse has a polymorphic wide tachycardia twisting around the baseline and a blood pressure of 88/50. Which action is correct?
choices: Synchronized cardioversion at 100 J
Adenosine 6 mg rapid IV push
Magnesium sulfate 2 g IV with correction of potassium
Diltiazem 0.25 mg/kg IV
checks.why: Torsades with a pulse is treated with magnesium and electrolyte correction while pads stay on. Synchronization fails on a shifting R wave, so if the pulse is lost the shock is unsynchronized. Adenosine and diltiazem have no role.

lessons.title: Electrolytes and toxins, second pass: the treatment side
lessons.body:
## Hyperkalemia, in the order you give it

The ECG tells you how urgent the potassium is; the number tells you how much work is left.

1. **Protect the membrane.** Calcium gluconate `1-3 g IV` over `5-10` minutes, or calcium chloride `0.5-1 g` through a central line. It works within `1-3` minutes, lasts `30-60` minutes, and does **not** lower potassium at all.
2. **Shift it into cells.** Regular insulin `10 units IV` with dextrose `25 g`, checking glucose afterward; albuterol `10-20 mg` nebulized, which is four to eight times the asthma dose; sodium bicarbonate only when the patient is genuinely acidemic.
3. **Remove it.** Dialysis is definitive. A loop diuretic helps only if urine is being made. Oral binders handle the subacute problem, not the emergency.

> **Trap:** The ECG arbitrates, not the laboratory value. A hemolyzed specimen reports a high potassium with a completely normal tracing, and a chronically uremic patient may look calm at `6.8`. A wide, slow, P-less rhythm at `6.0` is the emergency.

## Calcium moves the ST segment's length

**Hypocalcemia** stretches the ST segment, so the QT lengthens while the T wave itself stays normal-looking and simply arrives late. The two settings that produce it fast are **massive transfusion**, where citrate binds calcium, and injury to the parathyroid glands during neck surgery.

**Hypercalcemia** shortens the ST segment until the T wave appears to start straight off the QRS, giving a short QT. Malignancy and hyperparathyroidism are the usual causes.

## Sodium channel blockade has its own signature

Four findings travel together:

- QRS wider than `100 ms`
- a **terminal R wave in `aVR` taller than `3 mm`**
- an R-to-S ratio in `aVR` greater than `0.7`
- a rightward shift of the terminal `40` milliseconds of the QRS

The drug list is longer than most people expect: tricyclic antidepressants, diphenhydramine, cocaine, flecainide and propafenone, bupropion, carbamazepine, and hydroxychloroquine.

Treatment is **sodium bicarbonate `1-2 mEq/kg`** as boluses, repeated until the QRS narrows. A QRS over `100 ms` predicts seizures and a QRS over `160 ms` predicts ventricular arrhythmia, which makes the width a triage tool as well as a diagnosis.

## Digoxin, and why potassium decides

Digoxin increases automaticity while slowing AV conduction, so it can produce nearly any rhythm. The nearly specific ones are **atrial tachycardia with block**, **bidirectional ventricular tachycardia**, and an accelerated junctional rhythm in a patient who should be in atrial fibrillation.

In **acute** poisoning the potassium **rises**, because the sodium-potassium pump is poisoned, and a potassium above roughly `5.0-5.5 mEq/L` is a marker of severe toxicity and a trigger for digoxin-specific antibody fragments. In **chronic** toxicity the potassium is often low, which makes the toxicity worse.

## Beta blocker versus calcium channel blocker overdose

Both produce bradycardia, hypotension, junctional escape rhythms and AV block. One laboratory value separates them: beta blocker overdose tends toward **low** glucose, calcium channel blocker overdose toward **high** glucose, because calcium channels drive insulin release from the pancreas.

Treatment overlaps: calcium, **glucagon `3-5 mg IV`**, and **high-dose insulin with euglycemia**, commonly `1 unit/kg` bolus then an infusion titrated upward with dextrose support, plus vasopressors and lipid emulsion for refractory cases.

## Magnesium and temperature

**Hypomagnesemia** lengthens the QT and makes potassium impossible to replace; suspect it in every torsades. **Hypermagnesemia** prolongs PR, QRS and QT, blunts reflexes around `7-10 mg/dL`, and causes heart block and arrest at higher levels. Calcium is the antidote for both extremes of the membrane problem.

**Hypothermia** brings the Osborn wave, bradycardia, prolonged intervals, and atrial fibrillation around `32` degrees Celsius. Below `30` degrees the myocardium is irritable and defibrillation often fails, so the priority is gentle handling and active rewarming while resuscitation continues.
keyPoints: Hyperkalemia order: calcium to protect the membrane within minutes, then insulin with dextrose and albuterol to shift, then dialysis to remove
The ECG decides urgency in hyperkalemia; a hemolyzed sample gives a high number with a normal tracing
Sodium channel blockade: QRS over 100 ms, terminal R in aVR over 3 mm, R/S in aVR over 0.7, treated with sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mEq/kg
Acute digoxin poisoning raises potassium, and a level above roughly 5.0-5.5 mEq/L marks severe toxicity
Beta blocker overdose tends to low glucose and calcium channel blocker overdose to high glucose; both get calcium, glucagon, and high-dose insulin

checks.q: A patient has a potassium of 7.2 with a QRS of 0.16 and no visible P waves. What is given first and why?
choices: Insulin and dextrose, because shifting potassium is the fastest fix
Calcium, because it stabilizes the myocardium within minutes even though it does not lower potassium
Sodium bicarbonate, because it both shifts potassium and widens the therapeutic window
An oral potassium binder, because it removes potassium from the body
checks.why: Calcium raises the threshold potential and protects the myocardium within 1-3 minutes, buying time for the shifting agents. Insulin and albuterol take 15-30 minutes, bicarbonate only helps in acidemia, and binders are far too slow.

checks.q: An overdose patient has a QRS of 0.14 seconds with a 5 mm terminal R wave in aVR. What is the treatment?
choices: Sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mEq/kg boluses until the QRS narrows
Amiodarone 150 mg over 10 minutes
Calcium gluconate 1 g IV
Magnesium sulfate 2 g IV
checks.why: A wide QRS with a tall terminal R in aVR is the sodium channel blockade pattern, and hypertonic sodium bicarbonate overcomes the blockade. Amiodarone is itself a sodium channel blocker and would worsen it.

checks.q: An overdose patient is bradycardic and hypotensive with a serum glucose of 268 mg/dL. Which class is more likely?
choices: Beta blocker
Digoxin
Calcium channel blocker
Tricyclic antidepressant
checks.why: Calcium channels trigger pancreatic insulin release, so blocking them causes hyperglycemia. Beta blocker overdose tends toward hypoglycemia. Digoxin and tricyclics do not produce this glucose pattern with bradycardia.

lessons.title: Ten rhythm strips, written out
lessons.body:
## How to use this set

Each row gives you what you would measure off the paper: rate, regularity, P wave behavior, the PR and QRS intervals, and anything odd about morphology. Cover the right column, commit to an answer out loud, then check.

The discipline being trained is not recognition of a picture. It is the habit of saying rate, then regularity, then the P-to-QRS relationship, then widths, in that order, before naming anything.

## The strips

| # | What the paper shows | The read |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Rate `38`, regular, upright P before every QRS in `II`, PR `0.16`, QRS `0.08` | Sinus bradycardia. Treat only if the patient has symptoms caused by the rate. |
| 2 | P waves regular at `88`, QRS regular at `34`, PR different on every beat, QRS `0.16` | Third-degree block with a ventricular escape. Pace early; atropine acts above the lesion and will not work. |
| 3 | Ventricular rate `150`, regular, no clear P, sawtooth baseline in `II, III, aVF` at about `300`, QRS `0.08` | Atrial flutter with `2:1` conduction. The classic rate trap. |
| 4 | Rate `118`, irregularly irregular, no P waves, wavering baseline, QRS `0.09` | Atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response. |
| 5 | Rate `104`, irregular, at least three different P wave shapes with varying PR intervals, QRS `0.08` | Multifocal atrial tachycardia. Treat the lung disease, not the rhythm. |
| 6 | Rate `72` overall, every third beat early and wide at `0.16` with no preceding P and a full compensatory pause | Ventricular trigeminy. |
| 7 | Rate `82`, grouped beating, PR within each group `0.18`, then `0.26`, then `0.34`, then a P with no QRS | Mobitz I, Wenckebach. Block inside the AV node, usually benign. |
| 8 | P waves regular at `88`, every second P conducts with a constant PR of `0.20`, ventricular rate `44`, QRS `0.09` | `2:1` AV block. It cannot be typed from the strip, so treat it as potentially high grade. |
| 9 | Rate `188`, regular, QRS `0.16`, all complexes identical, independent P waves visible marching through, one narrow beat in the middle | Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia with AV dissociation and a capture beat. Both findings are confirmatory. |
| 10 | Rate about `230`, irregularly irregular, QRS width varying between `0.12` and `0.18` beat to beat, shortest R-to-R `220 ms` | Pre-excited atrial fibrillation. Procainamide or cardioversion; no AV nodal blockers. |

> **Trap:** Strips `4` and `10` are both irregular. The difference is width and speed, and confusing them is the error that leads to giving diltiazem to a WPW patient.

## What separated the hard ones

Strips `2`, `7` and `8` all involve dropped beats and they separate on the PR interval alone: variable and unrelated means complete block, progressively lengthening means Wenckebach, constant and every other beat means `2:1` and no classification.

Strips `6` and `9` both contain wide beats. Three or more consecutive wide beats is ventricular tachycardia by definition; one every third beat is trigeminy.

> **Key:** Every one of these ten was named with four measurements and one relationship: rate, regularity, QRS width, PR behavior, and where the P waves are. No picture recognition was required.
keyPoints: Name the rate, then regularity, then the P-to-QRS relationship, then the widths, before naming any rhythm
Dropped beats separate on the PR interval: progressive lengthening is Wenckebach, constant is Mobitz II, unrelated is complete block, 2:1 cannot be typed
A regular narrow tachycardia near 150 is flutter with 2:1 conduction until proven otherwise
AV dissociation plus a capture or fusion beat in a wide regular tachycardia confirms ventricular tachycardia
Irregular and narrow at 118 is atrial fibrillation; irregular and wide with varying width at 230 is pre-excited atrial fibrillation and is treated completely differently

checks.q: A strip shows P waves at 88, QRS at 34, a QRS width of 0.16, and a PR interval that differs on every beat. What is the correct management priority?
choices: Atropine 1 mg IV, repeating to 3 mg before anything else
Prepare transcutaneous pacing, because the escape is below the AV node
Adenosine 6 mg to unmask the underlying rhythm
Observation, since the rate is an adequate escape
checks.why: A wide escape at 34 in complete block is generated below the AV node, where atropine has no target. Pacing is the intervention; atropine may be tried but should not delay it, and adenosine has no role in bradycardia.

checks.q: Two strips are both irregularly irregular. One is at 118 with a QRS of 0.09, the other at 230 with QRS widths varying from 0.12 to 0.18. What is the key management difference?
choices: Both are treated with diltiazem, only the dose differs
The slower one needs immediate cardioversion and the faster one needs rate control
The faster one must not receive AV nodal blocking drugs and needs procainamide or electricity
Neither should be treated until the onset time is known
checks.why: The fast wide irregular rhythm with varying QRS width is pre-excited atrial fibrillation, where AV nodal blockers push conduction down the accessory pathway and can cause ventricular fibrillation. The narrow one is ordinary atrial fibrillation with a rapid response.

lessons.title: The two-minute read: ten twelve-leads against the clock
lessons.body:
## The drill

Set a timer for `120` seconds and force the whole read into it. The point is not speed for its own sake. It is that a time limit stops you from staring at the first abnormality and abandoning the search.

| Seconds | What you do |
|---|---|
| `0-10` | Calibration box, paper speed, then rate |
| `10-25` | Rhythm: regularity, and a P for every QRS |
| `25-40` | Intervals: PR, QRS, QT |
| `40-50` | Axis from leads `I` and `aVF` |
| `50-80` | ST and T lead by lead, in the four territory groups, checking for a mirror |
| `80-100` | Morphology: Q waves, R-wave progression, voltage, U waves |
| `100-120` | Say the read out loud in one sentence, then ask for the old tracing |

The closing sentence has a fixed shape, and saying it aloud is the part people skip: "Rate `96`, sinus rhythm, normal axis, PR `0.16`, QRS `0.09`, QTc `420`, `2 mm` ST elevation in `II`, `III` and `aVF` with reciprocal depression in `I` and `aVL`, which is an inferior STEMI."

## Ten tracings

| # | What the twelve-lead shows | The read |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Rate `82`, sinus, PR `0.14`, QRS `0.10`, `3 mm` elevation `V2-V4`, `1.5 mm` elevation `aVL`, `1 mm` depression `II, III, aVF` | Proximal LAD occlusion. Largest territory, highest shock risk. |
| 2 | Rate `48`, sinus, `2 mm` elevation `II, III, aVF` with `III` greater than `II`, `2 mm` depression `I` and `aVL`, `1 mm` elevation `V1` | Right coronary inferior STEMI with right ventricular involvement. Get `V4R`, give fluid, hold nitrates. |
| 3 | Rate `96`, sinus, PR segment depression in the limb leads with PR elevation in `aVR`, concave elevation in seven leads, no reciprocal depression | Acute pericarditis. |
| 4 | Rate `104`, sinus, `2 mm` horizontal depression `V1-V3` with an R taller than the S is deep in `V2` and upright T waves, `1 mm` elevation `II, III, aVF` | Inferoposterior infarction. Get `V7-V9`. |
| 5 | Rate `88`, sinus, QRS `0.14`, broad notched R in `V6`, `QS` in `V1`, `3 mm` elevation in `V5` in the same direction as the QRS | Left bundle branch block with concordant elevation. Sgarbossa positive, treat as occlusion. |
| 6 | Rate `62`, sinus, pain free, biphasic T waves in `V2-V3` rising then descending, R waves preserved, no Q waves | Wellens type A. Critical proximal LAD stenosis. Catheterization, not a stress test. |
| 7 | Rate `112`, sinus tachycardia, T inversions `V1-V4` and in `III`, incomplete right bundle branch block, deep S in `I` with Q and inverted T in `III` | Acute right heart strain. Supports pulmonary embolism; never excludes it. |
| 8 | Rate `44`, QRS `0.18`, no identifiable P waves, tall peaked narrow-based T waves `V2-V4` | Hyperkalemia. Calcium now, before the confirmatory number. |
| 9 | Rate `70`, sinus, `1.5 mm` elevation in `aVR`, `2 mm` depression in `I`, `II`, `aVL`, `V4-V6` | Left main or three-vessel disease, or global supply-demand failure. |
| 10 | Rate `126`, regular, PR `0.09`, QRS `0.12` with a slurred upstroke, tall R in `V1` | Wolff-Parkinson-White pattern with pre-excitation. |

## What the clock taught

Tracings `2` and `4` were both inferior, and both needed extra leads that no one orders unless the first read was systematic. Tracing `5` hides an occlusion under a bundle branch block, and tracing `8` hides one under nothing at all, because hyperkalemia is not an occlusion and gets mistreated as one when the search stops at the wide QRS.

> **Key:** The time limit is a search discipline, not a speed contest. Two minutes forces you past the first abnormality to the second one, which is where the diagnosis usually lives.

> **On shift:** A tracing you cannot name in two minutes is a tracing you hand to a provider immediately, saying what you measured. "Rate `44`, QRS looks very wide, no P waves I can find" is a useful sentence even when the name is not there yet.
keyPoints: Budget the read: 10 seconds calibration and rate, 15 rhythm, 15 intervals, 10 axis, 30 ST and T, 20 morphology, 20 for the spoken summary
Close every read with one spoken sentence in a fixed order, then ask for the prior tracing
Inferior patterns frequently need V4R or V7-V9, and nobody orders those leads unless the first pass was systematic
Concordant ST elevation inside a left bundle branch block is Sgarbossa positive and is treated as an occlusion
A wide QRS with peaked T waves and absent P waves is hyperkalemia, not a bundle branch block, and calcium comes before the confirmatory potassium

checks.q: In the two-minute structure, what is the last thing done before the tracing is set down?
choices: Measuring the QT interval
Checking the calibration box
Saying the read aloud in one sentence and asking for the prior ECG
Calculating the axis
checks.why: The spoken one-sentence summary forces the findings into a structure and exposes gaps, and comparison to an old tracing is the step that converts a finding into new or chronic. Calibration is first, not last.

checks.q: A tracing shows a QRS of 0.18 at a rate of 44, no P waves, and tall narrow-based peaked T waves. What is the biggest risk if the read stops at the wide QRS?
choices: Calling it a bundle branch block and missing hyperkalemia that needs calcium within minutes
Calling it ventricular tachycardia and shocking a perfusing patient
Calling it a paced rhythm and placing a magnet
Calling it pericarditis and giving anti-inflammatories
checks.why: Wide QRS plus absent P waves plus peaked T waves is the hyperkalemia progression, and calcium is time-critical. The rate of 44 makes ventricular tachycardia untenable, and neither pacing nor pericarditis fits the description.

cards.front: What separates an accelerated rhythm from an escape rhythm?
cards.back: An escape rhythm appears because nothing faster is available. An accelerated rhythm appears because a lower focus started firing faster than the sinus node and stole the beat.

cards.front: Describe accelerated junctional rhythm and name its usual causes.
cards.back: Regular, narrow, 60-100, with P waves inverted in II, buried in the QRS, or just after it. Causes: digoxin toxicity, inferior MI, myocarditis, first day after cardiac surgery, theophylline.

cards.front: How do you tell AV dissociation by usurpation from complete heart block?
cards.back: In block the atrial rate is faster than the ventricular rate and P waves fail on ready tissue. In usurpation the ventricular rate equals or exceeds the atrial rate, so no P gets a fair chance.

cards.front: What does ectopic atrial tachycardia look like, and how does it respond to adenosine?
cards.back: Rate 130-250 with a visible P wave of abnormal shape before every QRS and a warm-up onset. Adenosine usually exposes the P waves by blocking the AV node without stopping the tachycardia.

cards.front: How do you prove that an irregular narrow rhythm is flutter with variable block rather than atrial fibrillation?
cards.back: The flutter-to-flutter interval stays fixed near 0.20 seconds and every R-to-R interval is a whole multiple of it, so rates cluster at 150, 100 and 75 instead of scattering.

cards.front: What does sinus node dysfunction include?
cards.back: Inappropriate sinus bradycardia, sinus pauses, chronotropic incompetence, and tachy-brady syndrome in which atrial fibrillation stops and leaves a long pause before the sinus node recovers.

cards.front: How does sinoatrial exit block differ from sinus arrest on the strip?
cards.back: In exit block the pause is an exact multiple of the underlying P-to-P interval, because a beat formed and never escaped. In sinus arrest the pause has no arithmetic relationship, because no beat formed.

cards.front: What is the Ashman phenomenon and why does it happen?
cards.back: In atrial fibrillation, a long R-to-R followed by a short one produces one wide beat with an RSR' in V1. The right bundle has the longest refractory period, so an early beat conducts with a right bundle pattern.

cards.front: What is bidirectional ventricular tachycardia and what causes it?
cards.back: The QRS axis alternates beat to beat, upright then inverted in the limb leads. Causes: digoxin toxicity, catecholaminergic polymorphic VT, and aconite poisoning.

cards.front: How do you recognize pre-excited atrial fibrillation on a strip, and what is forbidden?
cards.back: Irregularly irregular, wide, very fast, with QRS width changing beat to beat and a shortest R-to-R under 250 ms. Give procainamide or electricity. Never adenosine, beta blockers, calcium channel blockers or digoxin.

cards.front: Why is ST depression in aVL worth chasing in a chest pain patient?
cards.back: aVL and lead III point almost exactly opposite one another, so aVL depression is often the earliest sign of an inferior occlusion, appearing before the inferior elevation is convincing.

cards.front: Which findings separate a right coronary from a circumflex inferior STEMI?
cards.back: Right coronary: III greater than II, depression in I and aVL, bradycardia or block, right ventricular involvement. Circumflex: II at least equal to III, I and aVL isoelectric or elevated, lateral and posterior changes.

cards.front: How is right ventricular infarction confirmed, and what is the diagnostic threshold?
cards.back: Right-sided leads: 0.5 mm of ST elevation in V4R is diagnostic, 1 mm in men under 30. ST elevation in V1 alongside inferior elevation is the clue on a standard tracing.

cards.front: What is the management of a right ventricular infarct?
cards.back: Give 500-1000 mL of crystalloid because the patient is preload-dependent, withhold nitrates and preload-lowering morphine, and expect AV block from the proximal right coronary lesion.

cards.front: Which findings mark a proximal rather than distal LAD occlusion?
cards.back: Anterior elevation V1-V4 plus elevation in aVL, reciprocal depression in II, III and aVF, often new right bundle branch block with left anterior fascicular block, and ST elevation in aVR.

cards.front: What is a wrap-around LAD and how does it look on the ECG?
cards.back: A long LAD that curls around the apex onto the inferior wall, so it produces anterior and inferior ST elevation at the same time, which looks contradictory until you know the anatomy.

cards.front: What pattern indicates a first diagonal occlusion?
cards.back: Elevation in I and aVL with reciprocal depression in III and aVF. With V2 elevation added and III depressed, the lead pattern is nicknamed the South African flag sign.

cards.front: Give the four findings of a posterior infarction in V1 to V3.
cards.back: Horizontal ST depression, an R wave taller than the S wave is deep in V2, an R wave 0.04 seconds or wider, and an upright T wave. Confirm with V7-V9 at 0.5 mm.

cards.front: How do you separate posterior infarct depression from ordinary subendocardial ischemia?
cards.back: Posterior depression is horizontal and maximal in V2-V3 with tall R waves and upright T waves. Subendocardial ischemia spreads more evenly across the precordium and lacks the tall R.

cards.front: Does a small territory mean a less urgent occlusion?
cards.back: No. A first diagonal occlusion involves only I and aVL, and a posterior infarct shows only depression on a standard tracing. Both are complete occlusions and are treated as such.

cards.front: Why does a newborn's ECG look right-dominant?
cards.back: In fetal life the right ventricle pumps against systemic resistance, so at birth the axis is +60 to +180 degrees with tall R waves in V1 and an R-to-S ratio in V1 greater than 1.

cards.front: What is the juvenile T wave pattern, and which finding is abnormal?
cards.back: The T wave in V1 inverts around day 7 and stays inverted until roughly age 7 or later. An upright T in V1 between one week and about seven years suggests right ventricular hypertrophy.

cards.front: Give normal resting heart rates for a newborn, a 4-year-old, and a 10-year-old.
cards.back: Newborn 110-160, 3 to 5 years 80-120, 6 to 12 years 70-110. Adolescents reach the adult 60-100 range.

cards.front: Do PR, QRS and QTc limits all change with age in children?
cards.back: PR and QRS upper limits are shorter in children and grow with age, roughly PR 0.12 to 0.18 s and QRS 0.07 to 0.10 s. QTc thresholds do not change: over 500 ms is high risk at any age.

cards.front: How do you distinguish infant SVT from infant sinus tachycardia?
cards.back: SVT is 220-300, metronome-regular with no beat-to-beat variation and absent or abnormal P waves. Sinus tachycardia rarely exceeds 220, varies beat to beat, and tracks fever, pain or volume loss.

cards.front: Give the pediatric adenosine, cardioversion and defibrillation doses.
cards.back: Adenosine 0.1 mg/kg then 0.2 mg/kg, maximum 6 mg then 12 mg. Synchronized cardioversion 0.5-1 J/kg then 2 J/kg. Defibrillation 2 J/kg then 4 J/kg, later shocks 4-10 J/kg.

cards.front: Why is bradycardia in a child treated with ventilation before drugs?
cards.back: Children depend on rate for cardiac output and their bradycardia is nearly always hypoxic. Oxygen and effective ventilation come first, compressions start under 60 with poor perfusion, then epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg.

cards.front: When is an RSR' in V1 a normal pediatric variant?
cards.back: When the QRS is narrow. With a wide QRS or right axis deviation the same pattern suggests right ventricular volume overload, classically an atrial septal defect.

cards.front: Which history features suggest congenital long QT syndrome in a child?
cards.back: Syncope with exertion, swimming, or a startling noise; a family history of sudden death or unexplained drowning; congenital deafness in the Jervell and Lange-Nielsen form.

cards.front: What do the first three positions of the NBG pacemaker code mean?
cards.back: Position I is the chamber paced, position II the chamber sensed, position III the response to a sensed event: I inhibited, T triggered, D both, O none.

cards.front: What does VVI mean and when is it used?
cards.back: Paces the ventricle, senses the ventricle, and an intrinsic beat inhibits the next paced one. It is the standard choice for atrial fibrillation with a slow ventricular response.

cards.front: What is DOO or VOO mode, and when do you want it?
cards.back: Asynchronous pacing at a fixed rate with no sensing at all. It is what a magnet produces and what is wanted during electrocautery, where interference could otherwise inhibit pacing.

cards.front: Name the four spike-and-complex combinations seen on a dual-chamber strip.
cards.back: Both paced; atrial paced with the patient's own QRS; the patient's own P with a paced ventricle, called atrial tracking; and fully inhibited with no spikes at all.

cards.front: What should a right ventricular paced QRS look like, and what does a tall R in V1 mean?
cards.back: A right ventricular paced beat looks like left bundle branch block with left axis. A tall R in V1 on a paced beat means the left ventricle is being paced, expected in a biventricular device.

cards.front: What causes failure to capture?
cards.back: Lead dislodgement or fracture, a rising threshold at the lead tip, hyperkalemia, class I antiarrhythmics, infarction under the lead, and battery depletion. Raising output or correcting potassium often restores it.

cards.front: What does undersensing look like and why is it dangerous?
cards.back: Spikes appear where the device should have been inhibited, marching into the patient's own beats. The danger is a pacing spike landing on a T wave, which can trigger ventricular fibrillation.

cards.front: What causes oversensing and how does it show on the strip?
cards.back: The device counts noise as beats and withholds pacing, producing pauses. Causes: T-wave oversensing, diaphragmatic or pectoral muscle potentials, electromagnetic interference, and a fractured lead.

cards.front: What is pacemaker-mediated tachycardia and how is it stopped?
cards.back: A paced ventricular beat conducts backward, the atrial channel senses the retrograde P, and the device paces again. It runs at the upper rate limit, often 110-130. A magnet breaks it instantly.

cards.front: What does a magnet do to a pacemaker versus an ICD, and what does a low magnet rate mean?
cards.back: Pacemaker: asynchronous DOO or VOO at the magnet rate, often 85-100. ICD: suspends shock therapy only, pacing unchanged. A magnet rate near 65 signals battery replacement time.

cards.front: What causes inappropriate ICD shocks, and what is electrical storm?
cards.back: Atrial fibrillation with a fast response, sinus tachycardia above the rate cutoff, T-wave oversensing, or lead fracture noise. Electrical storm is three or more shocks in 24 hours and is an emergency.

cards.front: Which two questions choose the ACLS branch, regardless of rhythm?
cards.back: Is there a pulse, and is the patient unstable because of the rhythm. Instability means hypotension, altered mental status, shock, ischemic chest pain, or acute heart failure.

cards.front: Give the full drug and energy sequence for shockable arrest.
cards.back: Defibrillate 120-200 J biphasic and resume compressions immediately, epinephrine 1 mg IV or IO every 3-5 minutes, amiodarone 300 mg after the third shock then 150 mg, rhythm check every 2 minutes.

cards.front: How does the QRS shape in PEA point at the cause?
cards.back: Narrow and fast suggests a filling or mechanical problem: hypovolemia, tamponade, tension pneumothorax, pulmonary embolism. Wide and slow suggests metabolic or toxic: hyperkalemia, sodium channel blockade, hypoxia, acidosis.

cards.front: What is the treatment for an unstable regular narrow tachycardia at 190 with a blood pressure of 72/40?
cards.back: Synchronized cardioversion at 50-100 J with sedation if there is time. Adenosine is acceptable only if line and drug are already at the bedside and will not delay the shock.

cards.front: What energy converts unstable atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response?
cards.back: Synchronized cardioversion at 120-200 J biphasic. Onset time and anticoagulation matter for elective cardioversion, but instability overrides both.

cards.front: Give two antiarrhythmic options with doses for stable monomorphic VT.
cards.back: Amiodarone 150 mg over 10 minutes, or procainamide 20-50 mg/min until the arrhythmia stops, hypotension develops, the QRS widens by 50 percent, or 17 mg/kg is given. Sotalol is an alternative.

cards.front: Give the full treatment of torsades de pointes with a pulse.
cards.back: Magnesium sulfate 2 g IV over about 15 minutes, stop all QT-prolonging drugs, replace potassium toward 4.5 mEq/L, and consider overdrive pacing or isoproterenol for recurrences.

cards.front: Which two rhythms must never receive a synchronized shock, and why?
cards.back: Polymorphic VT and pre-excited atrial fibrillation. Both are irregular and wide, so the machine cannot find a consistent R wave to synchronize to and may fail to fire. Defibrillate unsynchronized.

cards.front: Give the three-stage order of hyperkalemia treatment with doses.
cards.back: Protect: calcium gluconate 1-3 g IV over 5-10 minutes. Shift: regular insulin 10 units with dextrose 25 g, albuterol 10-20 mg nebulized, bicarbonate only if acidemic. Remove: dialysis, loop diuretic, binders.

cards.front: Why does calcium come first in hyperkalemia if it does not lower potassium?
cards.back: It raises the threshold potential and protects the myocardium within 1-3 minutes, lasting 30-60 minutes, which buys time for insulin and albuterol that take 15-30 minutes to work.

cards.front: When the potassium number and the ECG disagree, which one do you act on?
cards.back: The ECG. A hemolyzed specimen reports a high potassium with a normal tracing, and a chronically uremic patient may look calm at 6.8. A wide, slow, P-less rhythm is the emergency.

cards.front: Which two clinical settings cause acute hypocalcemia with a long QT?
cards.back: Massive transfusion, where citrate in stored blood binds calcium, and injury to the parathyroid glands during neck surgery. The ST segment stretches while the T wave itself stays normal-looking.

cards.front: Give the four ECG findings of sodium channel blockade.
cards.back: QRS wider than 100 ms, a terminal R wave in aVR taller than 3 mm, an R-to-S ratio in aVR above 0.7, and rightward shift of the terminal 40 milliseconds of the QRS.

cards.front: Name six drugs that produce the sodium channel blockade pattern.
cards.back: Tricyclic antidepressants, diphenhydramine, cocaine, flecainide or propafenone, bupropion, carbamazepine, and hydroxychloroquine. Treatment is sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mEq/kg until the QRS narrows.

cards.front: What do a QRS over 100 ms and over 160 ms predict in tricyclic overdose?
cards.back: Over 100 ms predicts seizures; over 160 ms predicts ventricular arrhythmia. That makes QRS width a triage tool as well as a diagnostic finding.

cards.front: What happens to potassium in acute versus chronic digoxin toxicity?
cards.back: Acute poisoning raises potassium because the sodium-potassium pump is blocked, and a level above roughly 5.0-5.5 mEq/L marks severe toxicity. Chronic toxicity usually runs with a low potassium, which worsens it.

cards.front: Which three rhythms are nearly specific for digoxin toxicity?
cards.back: Atrial tachycardia with AV block, bidirectional ventricular tachycardia, and an accelerated junctional rhythm appearing in a patient who should be in atrial fibrillation.

cards.front: Which laboratory value separates beta blocker from calcium channel blocker overdose?
cards.back: Glucose. Beta blocker overdose tends toward hypoglycemia; calcium channel blocker overdose toward hyperglycemia, because calcium channels drive pancreatic insulin release.

cards.front: Give the treatment overlap for beta blocker and calcium channel blocker overdose.
cards.back: Calcium, glucagon 3-5 mg IV, and high-dose insulin with euglycemia, commonly 1 unit/kg bolus then an escalating infusion with dextrose support, plus vasopressors and lipid emulsion if refractory.

cards.front: In what order do you say the findings before naming any rhythm?
cards.back: Rate, then regularity, then the P-to-QRS relationship, then the QRS width and PR behavior. Naming happens after the measurements, never instead of them.

cards.front: How do the three dropped-beat patterns separate on the PR interval alone?
cards.back: Progressive lengthening then a drop is Wenckebach. Constant PR with a sudden drop is Mobitz II. PR different on every beat with independent rates is complete block. Constant PR every other beat is 2:1 and cannot be typed.

cards.front: A strip shows ventricular trigeminy. What exactly does that mean?
cards.back: Every third beat is a premature ventricular complex: early, wide over 0.12 seconds, with no preceding P wave and a full compensatory pause. Three or more in a row would instead be ventricular tachycardia.

cards.front: Which two findings inside a wide regular tachycardia confirm a ventricular origin?
cards.back: Independent P waves marching through the tachycardia, which is AV dissociation, and a capture or fusion beat, which proves a supraventricular impulse reached the ventricle mid-run.

cards.front: Why does 2:1 AV block escape classification from the strip?
cards.back: Mobitz I is defined by progressive PR lengthening across consecutive conducted beats, and in 2:1 conduction you never see two conducted beats in a row. Treat it as potentially high grade.

cards.front: Two strips are irregularly irregular: one at 118 narrow, one at 230 with varying width. What is the danger of confusing them?
cards.back: The first is atrial fibrillation with a rapid response, rate-controlled with diltiazem. The second is pre-excited atrial fibrillation, where diltiazem can push conduction down the accessory pathway and cause ventricular fibrillation.

cards.front: Give the two-minute read time budget.
cards.back: 10 seconds calibration and rate, 15 rhythm, 15 intervals, 10 axis, 30 ST and T by territory, 20 morphology, 20 for the spoken one-sentence summary and a request for the prior tracing.

cards.front: What is the point of a time limit on an ECG read?
cards.back: It is a search discipline, not a speed contest. A time limit stops you staring at the first abnormality and forces the search through to the second, where the diagnosis often lives.

cards.front: What shape should the spoken summary of a twelve-lead take?
cards.back: Rate, rhythm, axis, PR, QRS, QTc, then the ST and T finding with its reciprocal change, then the name. Said aloud in one sentence, then compared to the prior tracing.

cards.front: A twelve-lead shows LBBB with 3 mm elevation in V5 in the same direction as the QRS. What is that?
cards.back: Concordant ST elevation, the first Sgarbossa criterion, which is highly specific for acute occlusion underneath a left bundle branch block. Treat as an occlusion rather than dismissing the elevation as discordance.

cards.front: Which two of the ten timed tracings required extra leads, and which leads?
cards.back: The right coronary inferior STEMI needed right-sided leads including V4R, and the inferoposterior pattern needed posterior leads V7-V9. Neither gets ordered unless the first read was systematic.

cards.front: What do you say to a provider when you cannot name a tracing?
cards.back: Report the measurements, not a guess. Rate, QRS width, presence or absence of P waves, and anything striking about ST segments is useful information even without a diagnosis attached.

quiz.q: A patient two days after coronary bypass surgery has a regular narrow rhythm at 78 with P waves inverted in lead II appearing just after each QRS. The sinus rate earlier was 84. What is the rhythm?
choices: Junctional escape rhythm
Ectopic atrial tachycardia
Third-degree AV block with junctional escape
Accelerated junctional rhythm
quiz.why: A junctional rhythm at 78 is above the junctional escape range of 40-60, so the junction is firing faster than its intrinsic rate and has usurped the beat. Escape would be slower, and complete block requires a faster, independent atrial rate.

quiz.q: A monitor shows P waves at 92 and QRS complexes at 96, with the P waves slowly sliding into the QRS over several beats and reappearing afterward. The patient is asymptomatic. How is this described?
choices: Isorhythmic AV dissociation
Complete heart block
Mobitz I second-degree block
Wandering atrial pacemaker
quiz.why: The ventricular rate slightly exceeds the atrial rate, so no P wave ever reaches ready tissue. Nothing is blocked. In complete block the atrial rate would be the faster of the two, and Mobitz I would show progressive PR lengthening with dropped beats.

quiz.q: A narrow tachycardia at 168 is given adenosine 6 mg. The ventricular rate slows briefly, revealing abnormal P waves at 168 that continue throughout, and then the tachycardia resumes at the same rate. What was it?
choices: AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia
Atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction
Ectopic atrial tachycardia
Sinus tachycardia
quiz.why: An automatic atrial focus keeps firing when the AV node is blocked, so adenosine exposes the P waves without terminating the rhythm. AVNRT uses the node in its circuit and would have converted. Flutter waves would be at about 300, not 168.

quiz.q: A rhythm is irregular at an average of 96. Careful measurement shows an unchanging atrial deflection every 0.20 seconds, and every R-to-R interval is exactly two, three or four of those intervals. What is the rhythm?
choices: Multifocal atrial tachycardia
Atrial fibrillation with a controlled response
Atrial flutter with variable AV conduction
Sinus arrhythmia with premature atrial contractions
quiz.why: A fixed atrial cycle length of 0.20 seconds is an atrial rate of 300, which is flutter, and R-to-R intervals that are whole multiples of it mean the AV node alternates conduction ratios. Atrial fibrillation has no fixed atrial interval at all.

quiz.q: A patient with syncope has a Holter recording showing a 4.8 second pause that measures exactly three times the surrounding P-to-P interval. What does the arithmetic indicate?
choices: Sinoatrial exit block, where beats formed but failed to leave the node
Sinus arrest, where no beat formed at all
A blocked premature atrial contraction
Mobitz II second-degree AV block
quiz.why: A pause that is an exact multiple of the underlying P-to-P interval means the sinus node kept firing on schedule and the impulses failed to exit. Sinus arrest produces a pause with no arithmetic relationship to the base cycle length.

quiz.q: In atrial fibrillation, a single wide complex with an RSR' pattern in V1 follows a long R-to-R interval that is immediately followed by a short one. What should this be called?
choices: The Ashman phenomenon, aberrant supraventricular conduction
A premature ventricular complex
A fusion beat
An escape beat from the right ventricle
quiz.why: Refractoriness depends on the preceding cycle length, so a long cycle followed by a short one catches the right bundle still recovering and produces a right bundle shaped beat. Calling it a PVC leads to unnecessary antiarrhythmic treatment.

quiz.q: A 26-year-old has an irregularly irregular wide tachycardia averaging 245, with QRS widths varying from 0.12 to 0.19 seconds and a shortest R-to-R of 210 ms. Blood pressure is 96/58. Which drug is most dangerous here?
choices: Procainamide
Amiodarone given slowly
Diltiazem
Magnesium sulfate
quiz.why: This is pre-excited atrial fibrillation. Diltiazem blocks the AV node, which removes the only brake on conduction and pushes impulses down the accessory pathway, risking ventricular fibrillation. Procainamide slows the accessory pathway and is the drug of choice.

quiz.q: A 58-year-old with chest pain has 1 mm of horizontal ST depression in aVL and no other clear abnormality on the first tracing. What is the most appropriate response?
choices: Reassure, since isolated aVL changes are non-specific
Order posterior leads V7 to V9
Diagnose a lateral wall NSTEMI and start heparin
Look hard at II, III and aVF and repeat the ECG in 10 minutes
quiz.why: aVL sits almost exactly opposite lead III, so aVL depression is often the earliest reciprocal sign of an evolving inferior occlusion. A repeat tracing captures the elevation as it develops. Posterior leads are for depression in V1 to V3.

quiz.q: Inferior ST elevation is present with lead II clearly larger than lead III, the ST segment in aVL is isoelectric, and there is 1 mm of elevation in V5 and V6. Which vessel is most likely?
choices: Left circumflex artery
Proximal right coronary artery
Left anterior descending artery
First diagonal branch
quiz.why: II at least equal to III, with no reciprocal depression in aVL and accompanying lateral elevation, points at the circumflex. A right coronary lesion gives III greater than II with reciprocal depression in I and aVL.

quiz.q: A patient with inferior ST elevation and 1 mm of elevation in V1 becomes hypotensive at 82/50 with clear lungs and distended neck veins. What is the correct immediate management?
choices: Sublingual nitroglycerin and intravenous morphine
Furosemide 40 mg IV for the distended neck veins
A 500 to 1000 mL crystalloid bolus while obtaining right-sided leads
Immediate synchronized cardioversion
quiz.why: Elevation in V1 with inferior elevation plus hypotension, clear lungs and distended neck veins is right ventricular infarction, which is preload-dependent. Fluid supports output, while nitrates, morphine and diuretics all drop preload and can cause collapse.

quiz.q: An anterior STEMI shows elevation in V1 to V4 plus 1.5 mm elevation in aVL, reciprocal depression in II, III and aVF, and a new right bundle branch block. What does this combination indicate?
choices: A distal LAD occlusion with a small territory
An occlusion proximal to the first septal perforator
A circumflex occlusion with anterior extension
A left main occlusion
quiz.why: aVL involvement with inferior reciprocal depression means the lesion is high on the LAD, and a new right bundle branch block implicates the septal perforator supplying the conduction system. A distal LAD spares aVL and produces no inferior reciprocal change.

quiz.q: A tracing shows 2 mm horizontal ST depression in V1 through V3 with R waves taller than the S waves are deep in V2 and upright T waves. What is the next step?
choices: Treat as anterior subendocardial ischemia with medical therapy
Obtain right-sided leads including V4R
Repeat the ECG in 6 hours
Place posterior leads V7 to V9 and look for 0.5 mm of elevation
quiz.why: Horizontal depression maximal in V2 to V3 with a tall R wave and upright T waves is the mirror image of posterior elevation. Posterior leads confirm it at a 0.5 mm threshold, and it is an occlusion, not a demand ischemia pattern.

quiz.q: An ECG shows 1.5 mm ST elevation in leads I and aVL only, with 1 mm of depression in lead III. There is no elevation anywhere else. How should this be handled?
choices: As a non-specific finding, since only two leads are involved
As pericarditis, because the elevation is limited
As an acute occlusion of a first diagonal or ramus branch
As left ventricular hypertrophy with strain
quiz.why: Two contiguous leads with elevation and a clear reciprocal mirror in III meet occlusion criteria. High lateral infarcts involve few leads and are frequently dismissed. Pericarditis is diffuse with no reciprocal depression except in aVR and V1.

quiz.q: A tracing shows ST elevation in V2 through V4 and simultaneously in II, III and aVF, with no reciprocal depression anywhere. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: Two separate simultaneous occlusions
A wrap-around LAD supplying both the anterior wall and the apical inferior wall
Acute pericarditis
Lead placement error
quiz.why: A long LAD that curls around the apex supplies the inferior wall distally, so one occlusion elevates both territories and the reciprocal changes cancel out. Pericarditis would show PR depression and concave morphology across most leads.

quiz.q: A 5-day-old infant has an ECG with a QRS axis of +140 degrees and a tall R wave in V1. How should this be interpreted?
choices: Right ventricular hypertrophy requiring urgent echocardiography
Lead reversal
Right bundle branch block
Normal for age, reflecting fetal right ventricular dominance
quiz.why: A newborn axis of +60 to +180 with a dominant R wave in V1 is the expected pattern, because the fetal right ventricle pumped against systemic resistance. It migrates leftward over the first few years.

quiz.q: A 4-year-old has an upright T wave in V1 on a preoperative ECG. What does this suggest?
choices: A normal juvenile pattern
Anterior ischemia
Right ventricular hypertrophy
Hyperkalemia
quiz.why: The T wave in V1 inverts around day 7 and stays inverted until roughly age 7. An upright T wave inside that window is abnormal and points at right ventricular hypertrophy. The normal finding at that age is inversion.

quiz.q: A 3-month-old is pale and feeding poorly. The monitor shows a narrow regular rhythm at 268 with no beat-to-beat variation and no identifiable P waves. What is the rhythm and the first drug?
choices: Sinus tachycardia from dehydration; give a 20 mL/kg fluid bolus
Supraventricular tachycardia; adenosine 0.1 mg/kg rapid IV push
Ventricular tachycardia; amiodarone 5 mg/kg
Atrial flutter; synchronized cardioversion at 2 J/kg
quiz.why: Infant sinus tachycardia rarely exceeds 220 and varies beat to beat with fever or volume state. A metronome-regular 268 with absent P waves is SVT, treated with adenosine 0.1 mg/kg then 0.2 mg/kg in a perfusing infant.

quiz.q: A 10-month-old with bronchiolitis has a heart rate of 46, mottled skin, and weak central pulses despite oxygen by mask. What comes next?
choices: Atropine 0.02 mg/kg IV
Transcutaneous pacing
Effective bag-mask ventilation, and chest compressions if the rate stays under 60 with poor perfusion
Adenosine 0.1 mg/kg
quiz.why: Pediatric bradycardia is nearly always hypoxic, so effective ventilation is the treatment and compressions begin at a rate under 60 with poor perfusion. Atropine addresses vagal causes and AV block, and pacing is rarely the first move in a child.

quiz.q: A 25 kg child in ventricular fibrillation needs defibrillation. What is the first energy dose, and what follows if it fails?
choices: 4 J/kg, so 100 J, then 8 J/kg, so 200 J
200 J, the adult dose, for any child over 20 kg
1 J/kg, so 25 J, then 2 J/kg, so 50 J
2 J/kg, so 50 J, then 4 J/kg, so 100 J
quiz.why: Pediatric defibrillation starts at 2 J/kg and escalates to 4 J/kg, with later shocks 4 to 10 J/kg without exceeding the adult dose. The 0.5 to 1 J/kg figures belong to synchronized cardioversion, not defibrillation.

quiz.q: A 15-year-old fainted while swimming and has a QTc of 505 ms. His younger brother drowned in a pool at age 9. What does this picture most strongly suggest?
choices: Vasovagal syncope with an incidental ECG finding
Congenital long QT syndrome
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome
quiz.why: Syncope triggered by swimming or a startling noise, a QTc over 500 ms, and a family history of unexplained drowning is the long QT picture. WPW shows a short PR with a delta wave, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy shows voltage with deep narrow lateral Q waves.

quiz.q: A device is programmed DDDR. What does the fourth letter add?
choices: Both chambers are paced and sensed
The right ventricular lead is the only pacing lead
Retrograde conduction is blocked
Rate modulation, so the device increases rate with activity
