quiz.why: The fourth NBG position is rate modulation, indicated by R, which lets the device raise the paced rate in response to a sensor such as motion or minute ventilation. The dual pacing and sensing are already described by the first three letters.

quiz.q: A strip from a dual-chamber pacemaker shows an atrial spike followed by a P wave, then the patient's own narrow QRS with no ventricular spike. What is happening?
choices: Failure to capture in the ventricle
Failure to pace from a depleted battery
Normal function: the intrinsic QRS inhibited the ventricular output
Oversensing of the T wave
quiz.why: In DDD mode, an intrinsic ventricular beat conducted through an intact AV node inhibits the scheduled ventricular output. That is the D in the third position working correctly, not a malfunction.

quiz.q: A paced patient has spikes appearing shortly after several of his own QRS complexes, one of which lands on a T wave. What is the malfunction and the risk?
choices: Undersensing, with a risk of an R-on-T induced ventricular arrhythmia
Oversensing, with a risk of prolonged pauses
Failure to capture, with a risk of asystole
Failure to output, with a risk of syncope
quiz.why: Spikes appearing where the device should have been inhibited mean it is not seeing the intrinsic beats, which is undersensing. A spike landing in the vulnerable repolarization window can trigger ventricular fibrillation.

quiz.q: A patient with a pacemaker and end-stage kidney disease misses dialysis and now shows pacing spikes with no capture on roughly half of the beats. What should be checked first?
choices: Lead fracture on chest radiograph
Serum potassium
Magnet rate
Device battery voltage
quiz.why: Hyperkalemia raises the myocardial capture threshold and is the most common rapidly reversible cause of failure to capture in a dialysis patient. Lead fracture and battery depletion are real causes but neither is correctable in the next ten minutes.

quiz.q: A patient with a dual-chamber pacemaker has a regular paced tachycardia at exactly 130 and is mildly symptomatic. A magnet is placed and the rate immediately becomes an asynchronous 90. What was the rhythm?
choices: Ventricular tachycardia
Sinus tachycardia with normal atrial tracking
Atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction being tracked
Pacemaker-mediated tachycardia at the upper rate limit
quiz.why: Retrograde conduction sensed by the atrial channel triggers repeated ventricular pacing, producing a rhythm parked exactly at the programmed upper rate limit. Removing sensing with a magnet breaks the loop instantly, which is the diagnostic test.

quiz.q: A patient with an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator is receiving repeated shocks while awake, alert and in atrial fibrillation at 170. What does a magnet placed over the device accomplish?
choices: It converts the device to asynchronous pacing and stops the arrhythmia
It suspends shock therapy while leaving pacing function unchanged
It reprograms the rate cutoff to a higher value
It turns the device off permanently
quiz.why: On an ICD a magnet suspends tachytherapy only and does not alter bradycardia pacing. On a pacemaker the same magnet produces asynchronous pacing. Neither effect is permanent, and the device still needs interrogation.

quiz.q: A patient with a biventricular resynchronization device previously had paced beats with a tall R wave in V1. Today the paced beats show a left bundle branch block pattern with left axis. What has changed?
choices: The left ventricular lead has stopped capturing
The device switched to asynchronous mode
The right ventricular lead has fractured
The patient developed hyperkalemia
quiz.why: A tall R in V1 on a paced beat indicates left ventricular capture. Losing it and reverting to a right ventricular apical pattern means only the right ventricular lead is capturing, which defeats the purpose of resynchronization therapy.

quiz.q: A monitored patient suddenly shows a chaotic waveform with no identifiable QRS and is unresponsive with no pulse. What is the correct first action?
choices: Two minutes of CPR before any shock
Epinephrine 1 mg IV, then defibrillate
Immediate defibrillation at 120 to 200 J biphasic, then immediate compressions
Synchronized cardioversion at 200 J
quiz.why: For witnessed, monitored ventricular fibrillation the defibrillator is already present, so immediate defibrillation is the priority and compressions resume at once without a pulse check. Synchronization is impossible without an R wave.

quiz.q: A patient in cardiac arrest has organized narrow complexes at 136 with no pulse, distended neck veins, and muffled heart sounds after recent cardiac surgery. Which reversible cause is most likely?
choices: Hyperkalemia
Sodium channel blocker overdose
Hypothermia
Cardiac tamponade
quiz.why: Narrow and fast PEA points to a filling or mechanical problem, and post-surgical distended neck veins with muffled sounds is tamponade. Hyperkalemia and sodium channel blockade produce wide, slow complexes instead.

quiz.q: A patient with a regular narrow tachycardia at 194 has a blood pressure of 70/38, cool skin and confusion. An IV has not been established yet. What is the correct action?
choices: Establish an IV and give adenosine 6 mg before anything else
Attempt a modified Valsalva maneuver
Synchronized cardioversion at 50 to 100 J with sedation if time allows
Start a diltiazem infusion
quiz.why: The rhythm is causing shock, so electricity is the treatment and establishing access must not delay it. Adenosine is reasonable only when the line and drug are already at the bedside; vagal maneuvers and rate-control infusions are for stable patients.

quiz.q: A patient has a monomorphic wide-complex tachycardia at 168, a blood pressure of 132/78, and is speaking in full sentences. Which plan is best?
choices: Immediate unsynchronized defibrillation
Pads applied, then amiodarone 150 mg over 10 minutes or procainamide 20 to 50 mg/min
Adenosine 12 mg as a first move to terminate it
Diltiazem 0.25 mg/kg IV to control the rate
quiz.why: A stable wide monomorphic tachycardia is treated as ventricular tachycardia with an antiarrhythmic while cardioversion is prepared. Diltiazem in a ventricular rhythm causes hypotension, and defibrillation is reserved for a pulseless or unstable patient.

quiz.q: A patient on methadone and ondansetron develops recurrent runs of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with a QTc of 570 ms. The runs stop spontaneously each time. What is the treatment plan?
choices: Amiodarone 150 mg over 10 minutes
Metoprolol 5 mg IV every 5 minutes
Synchronized cardioversion at 100 J
Magnesium sulfate 2 g IV, stop the offending drugs, replace potassium toward 4.5 mEq/L
quiz.why: Torsades is bound to a long QT, so the treatment is magnesium plus removal of every QT-prolonging drug and correction of potassium and magnesium. Amiodarone prolongs the QT further and would worsen it. Synchronization fails on a shifting R wave.

quiz.q: A patient with complete heart block has a ventricular escape at 32 with a QRS of 0.17 seconds, a blood pressure of 78/44, and is drowsy. Atropine 1 mg produces no change. What should happen next?
choices: Repeat atropine to the full 3 mg before any other therapy
Transcutaneous pacing, with dopamine or epinephrine as alternatives
Adenosine 6 mg to clarify the rhythm
Synchronized cardioversion at 100 J
quiz.why: A wide escape means the block is below the AV node, where atropine has no target, so pacing should not wait on repeated doses. Adenosine slows conduction further and cardioversion treats a tachyarrhythmia, not a bradycardia.

quiz.q: A dialysis patient has a potassium of 7.4, a QRS of 0.17 seconds, and no visible P waves. Which order of treatment is correct?
choices: Calcium gluconate, then insulin with dextrose and nebulized albuterol, then dialysis
Insulin with dextrose, then calcium, then a potassium binder
Sodium bicarbonate, then furosemide, then calcium
A potassium binder, then dialysis, then calcium if changes persist
quiz.why: Calcium protects the myocardium within 1 to 3 minutes without lowering potassium, which buys time for the shifting agents that need 15 to 30 minutes. Definitive removal by dialysis follows. Binders are far too slow for an emergency.

quiz.q: A laboratory calls with a potassium of 6.9 on a specimen noted to be hemolyzed. The patient's ECG is completely normal with visible P waves and a QRS of 0.08 seconds. What is the best interpretation?
choices: Give calcium immediately regardless of the tracing
Give insulin and dextrose and repeat the ECG in an hour
Start dialysis based on the level alone
The normal tracing argues for pseudohyperkalemia; redraw before treating a number
quiz.why: Hemolysis releases potassium from red cells in the tube, producing a high value with no physiologic effect. A completely normal tracing at a reported 6.9 should prompt a repeat draw. The ECG, not the number, defines the emergency.

quiz.q: A trauma patient receiving a massive transfusion develops a prolonged QT interval caused by a long flat ST segment while the T wave itself looks normal. What is the cause and the treatment?
choices: Hyperkalemia; give insulin and dextrose
Hypomagnesemia; give magnesium 2 g IV
Hypocalcemia from citrate binding; give calcium
Hypothermia; rewarm actively
quiz.why: Citrate anticoagulant in stored blood chelates calcium, and hypocalcemia lengthens the ST segment specifically, pushing a normal-looking T wave out to the right. Hypomagnesemia and hypothermia lengthen the QT differently and do not fit the transfusion setting as directly.

quiz.q: An overdose patient has a QRS of 0.15 seconds, a terminal R wave of 4 mm in aVR, and a heart rate of 128. Which treatment is indicated?
choices: Sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mEq/kg boluses until the QRS narrows
Amiodarone 150 mg over 10 minutes
Flumazenil 0.2 mg IV
Calcium chloride 1 g IV
quiz.why: A wide QRS with a tall terminal R in aVR is the sodium channel blockade signature, and hypertonic sodium bicarbonate overcomes the blockade with both a sodium load and alkalinization. Amiodarone is itself a sodium channel blocker and would worsen the picture.

quiz.q: An 80-year-old on digoxin for atrial fibrillation now shows a regular narrow rhythm at 72 with no fibrillatory irregularity, plus frequent ventricular ectopy. The potassium is 5.8. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: Successful rate control from the digoxin
Digoxin toxicity with regularized atrial fibrillation from an accelerated junctional rhythm
Conversion to sinus rhythm
A new complete heart block from ischemia
quiz.why: Atrial fibrillation that suddenly becomes regular is not conversion; it usually means complete AV block with a junctional focus taking over, a classic digoxin picture. The raised potassium supports acute toxicity and is itself a severity marker.

quiz.q: A bradycardic hypotensive overdose patient has a serum glucose of 42 mg/dL. Which ingestion is most consistent?
choices: Verapamil
Amitriptyline
Digoxin
Metoprolol
quiz.why: Beta blocker overdose impairs glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, producing hypoglycemia, while calcium channel blocker overdose blocks pancreatic insulin release and produces hyperglycemia. Digoxin and tricyclics do not cause this glucose pattern with bradycardia.

quiz.q: A hypothermic patient at 28 degrees Celsius in ventricular fibrillation does not respond to the first defibrillation attempt. What should guide the rest of the resuscitation?
choices: Repeat shocks every minute until conversion occurs
Continue CPR with active rewarming, since the cold myocardium resists defibrillation
Stop resuscitation, since survival is not possible below 30 degrees
Give three sequential shocks at maximum energy without compressions between them
quiz.why: A profoundly cold myocardium often will not convert until rewarmed, so the priority is high-quality CPR, gentle handling and active rewarming while attempts continue. Hypothermic arrest carries good neurologic outcomes, so resuscitation is not abandoned on temperature alone.

quiz.q: A strip shows P waves at 88 and QRS complexes at 34 with a QRS width of 0.16, and the PR interval is different on every beat. What does this rhythm require?
choices: Observation, because the escape rate is adequate
Atropine 1 mg, which will reliably increase the ventricular rate
Preparation for transcutaneous pacing, because the escape is below the AV node
Adenosine to slow the atrial rate and clarify conduction
quiz.why: Independent atrial and ventricular rates with a faster atrial rate means complete block, and a wide escape at 34 is generated below the AV node where atropine has no target. Pacing is the intervention and should not wait on drug trials.

quiz.q: A rhythm strip shows grouped beating with PR intervals of 0.18, 0.26 and 0.34 seconds within each group, then a P wave with no QRS after it. What is the rhythm and its usual course?
choices: Mobitz I, a block within the AV node that rarely progresses and often responds to atropine
Mobitz II, a block below the AV node requiring pacing
Third-degree block requiring immediate pacing
2:1 AV block that cannot be classified
quiz.why: Progressive PR lengthening ending in a dropped beat defines Wenckebach, which sits in the vagally innervated AV node. Mobitz II has a constant PR before the drop, and 2:1 conduction never shows two consecutive conducted beats to compare.

quiz.q: A wide regular tachycardia at 188 shows identical complexes, independent P waves marching through at 76, and a single narrow beat in the middle of the run. What do those two findings establish?
choices: Supraventricular tachycardia with aberrant conduction
Ventricular tachycardia, confirmed by AV dissociation and a capture beat
Atrial flutter with a bundle branch block
A paced rhythm with intermittent loss of capture
quiz.why: Independent P waves mean the atria and ventricles are not connected, and a capture beat proves a supraventricular impulse briefly reached the ventricles through the normal system. Both findings are essentially diagnostic of ventricular tachycardia.

quiz.q: A strip shows P waves at 88 with every second P conducting at a constant PR of 0.20 and a ventricular rate of 44. How should this be classified and managed?
choices: Mobitz I, treat conservatively
Sinus bradycardia with blocked premature atrial contractions
2:1 AV block, which cannot be typed from the strip and is treated as potentially high grade
Complete heart block requiring immediate pacing
quiz.why: Typing Mobitz I requires seeing PR lengthening across consecutive conducted beats, which 2:1 conduction never provides. Since it may be infranodal, it is treated as potentially dangerous. It is not complete block, because a fixed PR shows conduction is occurring.

quiz.q: Working through a timed read, you find PR segment depression in the limb leads, PR elevation in aVR, and concave ST elevation in seven leads with no reciprocal depression. What is the diagnosis?
choices: Anterolateral STEMI
Left ventricular aneurysm
Early repolarization
Acute pericarditis
quiz.why: PR depression with PR elevation in aVR, diffuse concave elevation crossing territories, and absent reciprocal change is pericarditis. A STEMI respects a vascular territory and shows a mirror. Early repolarization lacks PR segment changes.

quiz.q: A twelve-lead shows a QRS of 0.14 with a broad notched R in V6 and a QS in V1, plus 3 mm of ST elevation in V5 in the same direction as the QRS. How should this be treated?
choices: As a left bundle branch block with expected discordance, no action needed
As concordant elevation meeting Sgarbossa criteria, treated as an acute occlusion
As left ventricular hypertrophy with strain
As a paced rhythm requiring device interrogation
quiz.why: In left bundle branch block the ST segment should point opposite the main QRS deflection. Elevation of 1 mm or more in the same direction as the QRS is concordant, the first and most specific Sgarbossa criterion, and it means occlusion.

quiz.q: A timed read gives rate 70, sinus rhythm, 1.5 mm elevation in aVR, and 2 mm depression in I, II, aVL and V4 through V6 in a hypotensive patient. What does this pattern indicate?
choices: An isolated lateral STEMI
Posterior infarction
Acute pericarditis
Left main or severe three-vessel disease, or global supply-demand failure
quiz.why: ST elevation in aVR with depression in six or more leads reflects global subendocardial ischemia from left main or three-vessel disease. A lateral STEMI would show elevation in I and aVL with a mirror inferiorly, not diffuse depression.

quiz.q: During a two-minute read a tracing shows rate 126, a PR interval of 0.09 seconds, a QRS of 0.12 with a slurred initial upstroke, and a tall R wave in V1. What is the finding and what must be avoided if this patient later develops atrial fibrillation?
choices: Right bundle branch block; avoid beta blockers
Left ventricular hypertrophy; avoid nitrates
Pre-excitation from an accessory pathway; avoid AV nodal blocking drugs
Ventricular pacing; avoid magnet application
quiz.why: A short PR with a delta wave and a wide QRS is pre-excitation. If atrial fibrillation develops, AV nodal blockers remove the only brake on conduction and push impulses down the accessory pathway, risking ventricular fibrillation.

scenarios.title: Paced, and not capturing
scenarios.intro: A 74-year-old man is brought in by his daughter after two episodes of near-fainting at home this morning. He has a dual-chamber pacemaker placed in 2021 for sick sinus syndrome, end-stage kidney disease on hemodialysis, and he missed his session two days ago because of a snowstorm. He is pale and slow to answer but oriented. You are putting him on the monitor.

steps.prompt: The monitor shows pacing spikes marching at a regular `60` per minute, but only some of them are followed by a QRS. The effective ventricular rate is about `36`. He is awake and talking, but says the room feels far away.

choices.text: Get a 12-lead, place defibrillation pads for standby pacing, draw a basic metabolic panel including potassium
choices.feedback: Correct. Spikes without capture at a rate of 36 is failure to capture with a symptomatic patient. The 12-lead, the pads and the potassium all get moving at once because in a missed-dialysis patient the most likely reversible cause is chemical.

choices.text: Place a magnet over the device to force asynchronous pacing
choices.feedback: A magnet makes the device pace asynchronously, but it does not fix capture. If the myocardium will not answer a stimulus, pacing faster and blindly does nothing and removes sensing at the same time.

choices.text: Give atropine 1 mg IV for the bradycardia
choices.feedback: Atropine acts on the AV node. The problem here is that the muscle is not responding to a delivered stimulus, so atropine has no target and delays the real work.

steps.prompt: The 12-lead shows a paced rhythm with intermittent capture. Where the beats do capture, the QRS measures `0.19` seconds and looks broad and ill-defined. There are **no P waves** anywhere, and the T waves in `V2` to `V4` are tall, narrow-based and peaked. The potassium is still pending.

choices.text: Give calcium gluconate 1 to 3 g IV over 5 to 10 minutes now, before the potassium result
choices.feedback: Correct. Peaked T waves, absent P waves, a very wide QRS and failure to capture in a missed-dialysis patient is hyperkalemia until proven otherwise. Calcium protects the myocardium within 1 to 3 minutes. The number can confirm it afterward.

choices.text: Wait for the potassium result before giving anything
choices.feedback: The ECG is the faster test and it is already diagnostic. Waiting on a laboratory value while a patient shows a sine-wave trajectory is how these arrests happen.

choices.text: Call the device clinic to interrogate and increase the pacing output
choices.feedback: Raising output can restore capture and is a reasonable later step, but it treats the symptom. The threshold rose for a chemical reason that will keep worsening if untreated.

steps.prompt: Calcium is given. Within `3` minutes every spike captures and the rate is a paced `60`. He says the room came back. The potassium returns at `7.6` and the bicarbonate is `17`.

choices.text: Regular insulin 10 units IV with dextrose 25 g, albuterol 10 to 20 mg nebulized, and call nephrology for urgent dialysis
choices.feedback: Correct. Calcium bought 30 to 60 minutes and lowered nothing. The shifting agents move potassium into cells within 15 to 30 minutes, and dialysis is the only thing that removes it in this patient.

choices.text: Give an oral potassium binder and recheck in 4 hours
choices.feedback: Binders work over hours to days and are for the subacute problem. At 7.6 with capture failure, this is a dialysis-now situation.

choices.text: Give sodium bicarbonate 50 mEq IV as the sole shifting therapy
choices.feedback: Bicarbonate has a role when the patient is genuinely acidemic, and this bicarbonate of 17 qualifies, but it is weak and slow as a solo agent. Insulin with dextrose remains the workhorse.

steps.prompt: Nephrology is mobilizing a dialysis machine, which will take about `45` minutes. The patient is stable on a paced `60`. The daughter asks whether his pacemaker is broken and needs replacing.

choices.text: Explain that the device was working and the blood chemistry stopped the heart from answering it, keep pads on until after dialysis, and arrange device interrogation before discharge
choices.feedback: Correct on all three counts. The capture threshold rose because of potassium, not hardware. Pads stay on until the chemistry is fixed, and an interrogation documents thresholds and rules out a second problem.

choices.text: Tell her the pacemaker has failed and he will need a new generator
choices.feedback: This is almost certainly wrong and it is a distressing thing to say without evidence. Capture was restored by calcium, which points at physiology, not hardware.

choices.text: Remove the pads now that he is capturing and move him to a hallway bed
choices.feedback: He is one potassium shift away from losing capture again, and the dialysis has not started. Pads and a monitored bed stay until the cause is treated.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern to remember: failure to capture is not automatically a hardware problem. Hyperkalemia raises the myocardial capture threshold, and in a dialysis patient who missed a session it is the first thing to check and the first thing to treat. The tracing gave the answer before the laboratory did, because absent P waves, a very wide ill-defined QRS and peaked narrow-based T waves are a chemical picture, not an anatomical one. Calcium first, because it protects the membrane within 1 to 3 minutes and lowers nothing. Then shift with insulin, dextrose and albuterol. Then remove with dialysis, which is the only definitive step in anuric kidney disease. Pads stay on and the monitor stays connected until the potassium is actually down, and the device gets interrogated afterward to document that the hardware was never the problem.

scenarios.title: Wide, fast, and irregular
scenarios.intro: A 24-year-old woman walks into triage clutching her chest and saying her heart is doing something strange. She has had brief racing episodes since her teens that always stopped on their own. Nothing like this. She took no drugs, no stimulants, and had two cups of coffee. She is awake, anxious and pale, and triage brings her straight to a resuscitation room.

steps.prompt: The monitor shows a **wide** tachycardia that is clearly **irregular**, averaging about `240`. The QRS width is not constant; some complexes look `0.12` seconds wide and others closer to `0.18`. She is talking to you in short sentences.

choices.text: Get a 12-lead, apply defibrillation pads, establish two IVs, and have procainamide and the defibrillator ready
choices.feedback: Correct. Wide, irregular, very fast, with a QRS width that changes beat to beat is pre-excited atrial fibrillation until proven otherwise. Everything you prepare here is either electricity or a drug that slows the accessory pathway.

choices.text: Give adenosine 6 mg rapid IV push to see whether it terminates
choices.feedback: Dangerous. Adenosine blocks the AV node, which in pre-excitation removes the only brake on conduction and can accelerate the ventricular response into fibrillation. Adenosine is for regular narrow tachycardias.

choices.text: Give diltiazem 20 mg IV to control the rate since the rhythm is irregular
choices.feedback: The same error with a longer half-life. An irregular rhythm suggests atrial fibrillation, but a wide irregular rhythm with varying QRS width means the impulses are going down an accessory pathway, and calcium channel blockade pushes more of them there.

steps.prompt: The 12-lead confirms it: irregularly irregular, no organized P waves, QRS widths varying from `0.12` to `0.19` seconds, shortest R-to-R measured at `210` milliseconds, peak rate `280`. Her old records show a note from 2019 describing a short PR interval and a delta wave.

choices.text: Start procainamide 20 to 50 mg/min, stopping for hypotension, a 50 percent QRS widening, arrhythmia termination, or 17 mg/kg
choices.feedback: Correct. Procainamide slows conduction in the accessory pathway itself, which is the tissue actually carrying the fast beats. The stopping rules matter, because the drug is proarrhythmic and hypotensive if pushed past them.

choices.text: Give amiodarone 150 mg over 10 minutes as a broad-spectrum choice
choices.feedback: Amiodarone is a reasonable reflex in most wide tachycardias and a poor choice here. It has AV nodal blocking effects and has been reported to accelerate the ventricular response in pre-excited atrial fibrillation.

choices.text: Give metoprolol 5 mg IV to slow the rate while preparing for cardioversion
choices.feedback: Beta blockade is on the forbidden list for the same reason as adenosine, diltiazem and digoxin. Blocking the node favors the pathway.

steps.prompt: Ten minutes into the infusion her rhythm is unchanged and she is becoming drowsy. Her skin is cool and mottled to the knees.

choices.text: Synchronized cardioversion with sedation, escalating to unsynchronized defibrillation energy if the machine will not synchronize
choices.feedback: Correct. She has crossed into instability, so electricity replaces chemistry. Because the rhythm is irregular and the QRS shifts, the device may not find a consistent R wave, and in that case you deliver an unsynchronized shock rather than fight the machine.

choices.text: Continue the procainamide infusion past 17 mg/kg since it has not worked yet
choices.feedback: The stopping rules exist precisely for this. She is hypotensive and altered, and continuing the drug adds hypotension to a patient already in shock.

choices.text: Try adenosine now that the patient is deteriorating
choices.feedback: Deterioration does not change the pharmacology. Adenosine remains contraindicated in pre-excited atrial fibrillation, and the treatment for an unstable patient is a shock.

steps.prompt: She is sedated and shocked once. The rhythm converts to sinus at `88`. The post-conversion 12-lead shows a PR interval of `0.10` seconds, a slurred upstroke at the start of each QRS, and a QRS width of `0.12` seconds. She is awake and asking what happened.

choices.text: Admit for cardiology and electrophysiology evaluation for pathway ablation, document the drug contraindications prominently, and explain them to her
choices.feedback: Correct. She had a life-threatening episode from a pathway that can be ablated definitively. The contraindication list needs to follow her in the chart and in her own words, because the next clinician may only see an irregular tachycardia.

choices.text: Discharge on diltiazem for rate control with cardiology follow-up in two weeks
choices.feedback: This sends her home with the exact drug class that can kill her. Rate control agents that block the AV node are contraindicated in pre-excitation.

choices.text: Observe for six hours and discharge with no medication and a primary care referral
choices.feedback: Observation without an electrophysiology plan misses the point. A shortest R-to-R of 210 milliseconds marks a high-risk pathway, and she has already had one episode that required a shock.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern is three words: wide, fast, irregular. That combination, with a QRS width that changes from beat to beat and a shortest R-to-R under 250 milliseconds, is pre-excited atrial fibrillation, and it behaves unlike anything else on the monitor. The reason is anatomical. An accessory pathway connects atrium to ventricle without the AV node's protective delay, so every drug that blocks the node makes things worse by sending a larger share of fibrillatory impulses down the pathway. The forbidden list is adenosine, beta blockers, calcium channel blockers, digoxin, and in this setting amiodarone as well. What works is procainamide, which slows the pathway itself, and electricity, which resets everything. Instability decides between them, and an irregular rhythm with shifting complexes may defeat synchronization, in which case the shock is delivered unsynchronized at defibrillation energy. The definitive treatment is not a drug at all. It is ablation of the pathway, which is why the disposition is an electrophysiology conversation rather than a prescription.
